India’s New Deportation Policy

•The Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has formulated a new
 deportation policy to expedite identification and deportation of illegal migrants,
 particularly from Bangladesh and Myanmar.
•The policy, formalized through the Deportation Manual 2026 issued on April
 2, 2026, provides a standard operating procedure for detecting, detaining, and
 deporting illegal migrants.
•The move follows the Pahalgam terror attack (April 2025) and the
 regime change in Bangladesh (August 2024), which heightened focus on
 domestic security.

India’s New Deportation
                    Policy
What is Deportation? –
•Deportation is a formal legal process where a foreigner staying illegally is
 identified, detained, and removed from the country in accordance with law.
•Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, an “illegal migrant” is a foreigner who
 entered India without valid documents or stayed beyond the permitted period.
•Since citizenship falls under the Union List, the MHA oversees deportation and
 delegates responsibilities to state authorities.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Illegal migration began with large-scale movements during Partition (1947) from
 East Pakistan, followed by a major influx during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation
 War.
•Concerns over demographic changes led to the Assam Movement (1979–1985),
 demanding detection and deportation of illegal immigrants from Assam.
•The movement culminated in the Assam Accord (August 1985),
 fixing March 24, 1971 as the cut-off date for identifying illegal migrants.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Since the 1990s, porous borders with Bangladesh and Myanmar, along with
 economic and political instability, have sustained migration.
•The National Register of Citizens (NRC) for Assam, published in 2019,
 excluded nearly 19 lakh applicants as foreigners, but its implementation remains
 uncertain.
•The issue is now linked with security, identity politics, and resource pressures,
 prompting stricter measures like border fencing and deportation drives.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Unregulated migration may place pressure on public resources such as food
 distribution, healthcare, and housing.
•Large-scale undocumented influx alters local demographics, creating socio-
 political tensions with indigenous and tribal communities in border states.
•Possession of voter IDs by non-citizens raises serious questions about the
 sanctity of electoral rolls in high-migrant constituencies.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
National Register of Citizens –
•The NRC is an official register of Indian citizens in Assam, prepared under
 Supreme Court supervision with March 24, 1971 as the cut-off date, as per
 the Assam Accord (1985).
•The final NRC, published in 2019, included 3.11 crore persons out of 3.30
 crore applicants, excluding over 19 lakh people.
•The NRC has not been formally notified for nationwide implementation and
 remains limited to Assam.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Those excluded from the NRC can appeal before Foreigners’ Tribunals
 (FTs) , quasi-judicial bodies empowered under the Foreigners Act, 1946, to
 declare a person a foreigner.
•Over 1.65 lakh persons have already been declared foreigners by FTs, and
 more than 85,000 cases are still pending.
•FTs are unique to Assam and play a crucial role in the deportation process, as
 the new policy's holding centre guidelines apply to those declared foreigners by
 these tribunals.

India’s New Deportation
                   Policy
India’s Land Borders –
•India shares a total land border of approx. 15,106.7 km with seven
 neighbours: Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and
 Afghanistan.
•The longest border is with Bangladesh (4,096.7 km) and the shortest
 with Afghanistan (106 km).
•17 states and UTs have international borders; the BSF, ITBP and SSB guard
 different frontiers.

India’s New Deportation
                     Policy
•India’s coastline has been re-assessed from 7,516.6 km to 11,098.81 km by
 the National Hydrographic Office using modern GIS data.
•Gujarat has the longest revised coastline (2,340.62 km), followed by
 Tamil Nadu (1,068.69 km) and Andhra Pradesh (1,053.07 km).
•India’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) is approx. 2 million sq. km, extending
 200 nautical miles from the coast.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
Highlights of Policy–
•States must set up a special task force in each district under police
 supervision to detect, identify, and deport illegal migrants from Bangladesh and
 Myanmar.
•These task forces must submit a monthly status report to the Centre on
 foreigners who are missing or overstaying their visas.
•Task forces operate under the District Magistrate, who is designated as the
 competent authority to verify citizenship claims.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•An upper limit of 90 days is fixed to verify the antecedents of suspected
 Bangladeshi or Myanmar nationals.
•States must verify credentials of suspected illegal immigrants within 30 days;
 failure results in automatic deportation proceedings.
•If no credential report is received within 30 days, the Foreigners Registration
 Office can proceed with deportation.

India’s New Deportation
                        Policy
•States must set up holding centers with a 10-feet-high barbed wire boundary
 and strict access control for undocumented migrants awaiting deportation.
•Centers cannot be run from jails; private buildings can be hired if government
 land is unavailable. Basic amenities must be ensured.
•Crucially, members of the same family must not be separated and must be
 housed together.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•A dedicated Foreigners Identification Portal (FIP) has been launched to
 capture biometric and demographic details of intercepted illegal foreigners.
•The District Police Module (DPM) has been launched in over 700 districts to
 track illegal migrants efficiently.
•Data will be shared with UIDAI, the Election Commission, and the MEA to
 prevent future issuance of documents to deported individuals.

India’s New Deportation
                         Policy
•Documents obtained illegally by migrants, such as Aadhaar, PAN cards, and
 driving licenses, must be uploaded for cancellation.
•Deported individuals will be blacklisted by the Bureau of Immigration to
 prevent future entry into India.
•The Bureau of Immigration will publish a list of deportees on a public portal for
 transparency.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•Migrants intercepted at land or maritime borders will be immediately sent
 back after biometric capture, without court process.
•Inadvertent crossers, if found innocent after interrogation, may be handed over
 to border forces of respective countries.
•Illegal immigrants detected near the zero line or within 12 hours of entry
 will be pushed back immediately.

India’s New Deportation
                          Policy
•The guidelines for holding centers also apply to those declared foreigners
 by Foreigners’ Tribunals (FTs) , which are unique to Assam.
•Assam has over 82,000 cases pending in FTs, prompting a separate SOP
 under the Immigrants (Expulsion from Assam) Act, 1950.
•Under the new SOP, Deputy Commissioners can issue expulsion orders within 10
 days, bypassing lengthy tribunal processes.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 replaces four older laws: the
 1920 Passport Act, 1939 Registration Act, 1946 Foreigners Act, and 2000
 Carriers’ Liability Act.
•The Act mandates compulsory reporting of foreign nationals by hotels,
 educational institutions, and healthcare facilities.
•It provides statutory backing to the Bureau of Immigration to identify,
 detain, and deport illegal migrants.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Individuals using or supplying forged passports or visas may face 2 to 7 years
 of imprisonment and fines of ₹1 lakh to ₹10 lakh.
•Anyone entering India illegally without valid documents faces up to 5 years in
 prison and a fine of up to ₹5 lakh.
•The Act also introduces a statutory national floor wage under the Code on
 Wages (relating to labour law).

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•Under Article 258(1) , the Centre has delegated the power to identify and
 deport illegal foreign nationals to state governments.
•The Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964 empowers District Magistrates to
 set up tribunals to determine if a person is a foreigner.
•India is not a signatory to the UN Refugee Convention (1951) or its 1967
 Protocol, and states cannot grant "refugee" status.

India’s New Deportation
                        Policy
•Millions of Indians, especially those born before the mid-1980s, lack standard
 birth certificates, leading to harassment of genuine citizens.
•Cases have been reported where Indian citizens with Aadhaar and voter ID
 were deported to Bangladesh without proper verification.
•Police in several states insist on passports or birth certificates for proof of
 citizenship, which many poor families do not have.

India’s New Deportation
                              Policy
•Deportation requires the “parent country” (Bangladesh or Myanmar) to officially accept
 the individuals as their citizens.
•If the origin country denies nationality, individuals risk becoming stateless, languishing
 indefinitely in holding centres.
•Rohingya deportees face acute risk of statelessness, as Myanmar does not recognize
 them as citizens.

India’s New Deportation
                        Policy

•Holding centers have historically faced allegations of poor living conditions;
 prolonged detention of children and women raises ethical concerns.
•The principle of non-refoulement (not returning individuals to persecution) is
 part of international customary law, yet India's pushback policy violates it.
•Despite India’s election to the UN Human Rights Council (2026–28), such
 measures risk undermining its international image.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•District police and local administrations lack capacity and training for nationality
 verification within the strict 90-day timeline.
•This risks delays, increases case pendency, opens avenues for corruption, and
 disproportionately affects vulnerable groups.
•The Supreme Court has intervened in cases of wrongful deportation, directing
 repatriation of Indian citizens.

India’s New Deportation
                    Policy
•The government must ensure transparent verification using multiple data
 points to prevent harassment of genuine Indian citizens.
•Aadhaar, voter ID, land records, and school certificates should be accepted as
 valid proof of citizenship for marginalised communities.
•Technology like biometric databases should improve accuracy while
 guaranteeing procedural safeguards under Article 21.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•India must engage diplomatically to establish a streamlined SOP for smooth
 and timely acceptance of deported nationals.
•Bilateral repatriation agreements should be negotiated to prevent statelessness
 and ensure structured deportation.
•A domestic refugee law should be enacted to distinguish genuine asylum
 seekers from illegal economic migrants.

India’s New Deportation
                     Policy
•Preventing illegal infiltration at the source requires implementing the
 Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System (CIBMS) and
 smart fencing.
•India shares a free-border agreement with Nepal and a Free Movement
 Regime (FMR) with Myanmar (10 km on either side), requiring careful
 review.
•Strengthening documentation with robust verification mechanisms for Aadhaar
 and voter ID, including police checks, is essential.

India’s New Deportation
                             Policy
•The new deportation policy strengthens India’s legal and institutional framework to identify
 and remove illegal migrants, addressing security concerns and resource strains in
 border states.
•However, its successful implementation depends on transparent verification processes,
 respect for human rights, and effective diplomatic engagement with neighboring countries
 to prevent statelessness.
•Balancing national security imperatives with humanitarian obligations and protection of
 genuine Indian citizens remains the central challenge for policymakers.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•On April 14, 2026, the government circulated three Bills to pave the way
 for fresh delimitation, raise Lok Sabha strength to 850 members, and
 operationalize one-third reservation for women in Parliament and
 state Assemblies.
•The legislative package comprises the Constitution (131st Amendment)
 Bill, 2026, the Delimitation Bill, 2026, and the Union Territories Laws
 (Amendment) Bill, 2026.
•The Bills build on the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 (Nari
 Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), which had introduced women's reservation but
 linked its implementation to a future Census and delimitation exercise.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
What is Delimitation? –
•Delimitation means the act or process of fixing limits or boundaries of
 territorial constituencies in a country to represent changes in population.
•It involves readjusting the number of seats and boundaries of
 constituencies in each State for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative
 Assemblies, as well as determining seats reserved for SCs and STs.
•The purpose is to provide equal representation to equal segments of
 population and follow the democratic principle of "one person, one vote,
 one value."

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•Delimitation ensures that each seat represents roughly the same number
 of voters, preventing underrepresentation or overrepresentation of specific
 areas as population densities shift over time.
•It helps in fair division of geographical areas so that one political party does
 not gain an unfair advantage over others in an election.
•It is crucial for upholding the democratic principle of “one citizen-one
 vote-one value” and ensuring equitable distribution of seats among different
 regions.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•Under Article 82 of the Constitution, Parliament enacts a Delimitation
 Act after every Census, readjusting Lok Sabha seat allocation to States and
 dividing each State into territorial constituencies.
•Under Article 170, States are similarly divided into territorial
 constituencies as per the Delimitation Act after every Census, ensuring
 periodic readjustment at both central and state levels.
•This constitutional framework ensures that representation in Parliament and
 state Assemblies remains reflective of demographic realities over time.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
Delimitation Commission -
•The Delimitation Commission is a high-power body appointed by the
 President of India and works in collaboration with the Election Commission
 of India.
•It consists of three members: a serving or retired Supreme Court judge
 (appointed as Chairperson), the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election
 Commissioner nominated by them), and the State Election Commissioner of
 the concerned State.
•The Commission is designed to function without any executive influence,
 ensuring independence in the delimitation process.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The Commission has powers equivalent to a civil court for summoning
 witnesses, requiring production of documents, and receiving evidence.
•In case of a difference of opinion among members, the opinion of the
 majority prevails, ensuring efficient decision-making.
•The orders of the Commission have the force of law and cannot be
 questioned before any court once published, as judicial intervention
 would hold up elections indefinitely.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•Delimitation Commissions have been set up four times — in 1952, 1963,
 1973, and 2002 — under the Delimitation Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972,
 and 2002 respectively.
•The first delimitation exercise was carried out by the President (with the
 help of the Election Commission) in 1950-51, even before the first
 Delimitation Commission Act was enacted in 1952.
•There was no delimitation after the 1981 and 1991 Censuses due to the
 constitutional freeze imposed by various amendments.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The 2002 Delimitation Commission, also known as the Kuldip Singh
 Commission, redrew the internal boundaries of Lok Sabha and Vidhan
 Sabha constituencies using 2001 census figures.
•However, it was constitutionally prohibited from altering any state’s total
 number of seats, as the freeze on inter-state seat allocation remained in
 effect.
•As a result, while constituency boundaries were rationalised, the state-wise
 distribution of seats remained frozen at the 1971 Census levels.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
Constitutional Amendments (1976–2003) –
•The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, froze the total number of seats in the Lok
 Sabha based on the 1971 Census to ensure that states implementing
 population control measures were not penalised with reduced political
 representation.
•The amendment was passed to incentivise family planning policies,
 particularly in southern states that had successfully controlled population
 growth.
•This freeze was initially intended to last until the year 2000, giving states time to
 stabilise their populations without losing parliamentary seats.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The 84th Amendment Act, 2001, extended the freeze on the total
 number of seats until the first census after 2026, further protecting states
 that had achieved demographic transition.
•While inter-state seat allocation remained frozen, the 84th Amendment
 empowered the government to undertake readjustment and rationalisation
 of territorial constituencies in the states based on the 1991 census
 figures.
•This amendment allowed for internal redrawing of boundaries without
 altering any state's total number of Lok Sabha seats.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The 87th Amendment Act, 2003, provided for the delimitation of
 constituencies on the basis of the 2001 Census instead of the 1991
 Census.
•However, this could be done without altering the number of seats allotted
 to each state in the Lok Sabha, maintaining the freeze on inter-state
 distribution.
•These amendments collectively ensured that the inter-state seat
 allocation remained dependent on the 1971 Census until the first
 Census after 2026.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The freeze on seat allocation is now approaching its constitutionally
 mandated expiry and lifts automatically upon publication of the relevant
 figures for the first census taken after 2026.
•Once the figures of the ongoing census are published, realistically, between
 2029 and 2031, the freeze expires of its own terms under Article 82,
 without any further parliamentary action.
•The Delimitation Commission then constituted will work on pure population
 proportionality under the unamended Article 81(2)(a), and every state’s
 Lok Sabha allocation will reflect its share of the national population.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
Constitutional Provisions Related to Delimitation –
•Article 81 of the Constitution deals with the composition of the Lok
 Sabha, specifying the maximum number of representatives from states and
 Union Territories.
•The current provision caps the House at “not more than five hundred
 and thirty members” from states, plus up to 20 from Union Territories, a
 total upper limit of 550.
•The proposed 131st Amendment sought to amend Article 81 to
 increase this strength to 850 seats (815 from states and 35 from
 Union Territories).

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•Article 82 provides for the readjustment of the allocation of seats in the
 Lok Sabha to states and the division of each state into territorial
 constituencies after every census.
•The 131st Amendment Bill sought to amend the marginal heading of
 Article 82 from “Readjustment after each Census” to "Readjustment
 of constituencies", removing the mandatory link with every census.
•It also sought to remove the requirement of readjusting the number of Lok
 Sabha seats in states after every census, replacing it with executive
 discretion.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•Article 330 of the Constitution provides for reservation of seats for
 Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha.
•Article 332 provides for similar reservation in the Legislative Assemblies
 of the States.
•The delimitation exercise determines the allocation of reserved seats for
 SCs and STs based on their population concentration in each state, and
 any seat reallocation will affect these reservations as well.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•Article 334A was inserted by the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act,
 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), providing for one-third
 reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state Legislative Assemblies.
•The reservation was to be activated only after delimitation based on the
 first Census conducted after 2023, linking women's quota
 implementation to the delimitation exercise.
•The 131st Amendment Bill sought to operationalise this quota
 immediately after delimitation, but its failure has left women’s reservation in
 legislative limbo.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
The Delimitation Bill, 2026 –
•It provides the institutional framework for the exercise, creating a new
 Delimitation Commission headed by a Supreme Court judge, with the Chief
 Election Commissioner and State Election Commissioners as members.
•The Commission will be tasked with allocating seats across States, redrawing
 constituency boundaries, and determining reservations for Scheduled Castes
 (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and women.
•The Commission is given powers equivalent to a civil court, and its orders
 have the force of law, though the Bill provides for safeguards like draft
 publication, objections, and public hearings.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, failed to secure required
 majority, while 298 members voted in its favour and 230 against, the
 Bill needed 352 votes — two-thirds of the 528 present and voting — to
 pass.
•Following this defeat, the government withdrew the Delimitation Bill and the
 Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, marking a significant setback for the
 immediate operationalisation of women’s political reservation in India.
•The failure has reopened deeper debates on representation, federalism, and
 electoral restructuring, while leaving the constitutional freeze on
 delimitation to expire automatically after the post-2026 Census.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The proposed amendment seeks to remove the decades-old constitutional
 freeze that had fixed Lok Sabha representation to the 1971 Census, enabling
 delimitation based on the “latest published census figures” as may be
 notified by Parliament.
•The amendment raises the cap on elected members from states to 815 and
 from Union Territories to 35, significantly increasing the size of the House
 and altering the arithmetic of parliamentary majorities.
•The amendment enables a comprehensive redistribution of seats in line with
 current population patterns, effectively clearing the way for India's first
 inter-state seat redistribution since 1976.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The Bill sought to amend Article 81 to increase the maximum strength of
 the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 seats (815 from states and 35 from Union
 Territories), a 55% increase.
•It proposed to modify Article 82 to remove the mandatory link between
 delimitation and every census, enabling delimitation based on the “latest
 available census figures” (likely the 2011 Census).
•It also sought to amend Article 170 for state Assemblies and provisions
 related to SC/ST reservation, and to fast-track women's reservation by
 amending Article 334A to operationalise the 33% quota immediately
 after delimitation.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The Bill provides for safeguards such as draft publication, objections from
 stakeholders, and public hearings before the Commission finalises its
 orders.
•However, once notified, the Commission’s orders have the force of law
 and cannot be challenged in court under Section 10(2) of the
 Delimitation Act, 2002, which bars challenges to Commission
 orders.
•When the orders are laid before the Lok Sabha or State Legislative
 Assemblies, they cannot affect any modification, making the
 Commission's decisions final and binding.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
The Kishorchandra Rathod Case (2024) –
•In this landmark 2024 verdict, the Supreme Court asserted the power of
 judicial review over Delimitation Commission’s orders, marking a bold step
 towards fortifying democratic principles in electoral jurisprudence.
•The Court held that nothing ousts constitutional courts from scrutinizing the
 validity of orders passed by the Delimitation Commission on the touchstone of the
 Constitution.
•The ruling established that judicial review is available if an order is found to be
 “manifestly arbitrary” and “irreconcilable to constitutional values”.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The Court clarified that the complete bar on judicial intervention under
 Article 329(a) of the Constitution does not apply to cases where the
 Commission's order is manifestly arbitrary.
•The Court set aside the Gujarat High Court’s judgment which had
 declared a complete bar to judicial review of delimitation orders, opening a
 limited scope for constitutional scrutiny.
•This ruling provides a crucial check on the Delimitation Commission’s
 powers, ensuring that even though its orders are final, they cannot
 violate constitutional principles without judicial remedy.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•Southern states argue they are being punished for successfully implementing
 population control policies over the last 50 years.
•Under strict population proportionality, states like Uttar Pradesh and Bihar would
 gain seats significantly, while states like Tamil Nadu and Kerala would see their
 proportional share shrink or lose seats.
•Despite having only 18% of the country’s population, southern states contribute
 35% to national GDP; reducing their political representation creates a scenario akin
 to “taxation without adequate representation”.

The Delimitation Bill, 2026
•The failure of the 131st Amendment Bill means the constitutional freeze on
 delimitation will expire automatically after the post-2026 Census, and the
 Delimitation Commission will then work on pure population proportionality under
 unamended Article 81(2)(a).
•This would benefit high-growth states in the north and central India over
 demographically stabilised states in the south, creating a structural dilemma: how
 to balance democratic equality with federal safeguards for better-
 performing states.
